title: H-1B Wage Rule Reaches White House as Final Rule; Higher Floors Could Land in 2027
excerpt: OIRA received the Labor Department's prevailing-wage final rule on November 6. As proposed, entry-level H-1B wages would rise from the 17th to the 34th percentile.
body:
• The Department of Labor's final rule raising prevailing wages for H-1B, H-1B1 and E-3 workers and for PERM green-card cases was received by the White House's regulatory office (OIRA) on November 6, 2026 — the last checkpoint before publication.
  • As proposed in March 2026, the four wage levels would rise from the 17th, 34th, 50th and 67th percentiles to the 34th, 52nd, 70th and 88th percentiles; the final text has not been released and could differ.
  • Nothing changes today: the new wages would apply only from an effective date at least 60 days after Federal Register publication, so the earliest realistic effect is in 2027.
  • Under the proposal, labour condition applications filed before the effective date keep today's wage levels — employers with planned filings have a window to act, according to Immigration Analytics.

The Labor Department's plan to raise the minimum wages employers must pay sponsored foreign workers has reached its final checkpoint. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) logged the final rule — "Improving Wage Protections for the Temporary and Permanent Employment of Certain Foreign Nationals in the United States," RIN 1205-AC30 — as received on November 6, 2026, and lists it as economically significant and pending review, according to the OIRA entry summarised by Immigration Analytics.

Who is affected — exactly

The rule covers employers sponsoring workers in the H-1B, H-1B1 and E-3 nonimmigrant programmes, and employers running PERM labour certification — the first step in most employment-based green cards. It does not change visa eligibility, quotas or status; it changes the wage floor a sponsoring employer must offer or pay for a given occupation in a given area. Workers already employed under certified applications are not reopened by the change as proposed.

"In fiscal 2024, 19% of certified labour condition applications were at Level I and 44% at Level II, so the shift would be felt most at the entry and early-career levels."

What would change, precisely

Prevailing wages are set at four skill levels from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey: Level I (entry) at the 17th percentile, Level II at the 34th, Level III at the 50th and Level IV (fully competent) at the 67th. The March 2026 proposal would move those to the 34th, 52nd, 70th and 88th percentiles — in effect making today's Level II wage the new entry-level floor. The Labor Department's stated rationale is that the 2005 methodology set the levels too low and that higher floors better align sponsored workers' pay with comparable US workers, as the department's proposal is summarised by Legal 500. In fiscal 2024, 19% of certified labour condition applications were at Level I and 44% at Level II, so the shift would be felt most at the entry and early-career levels.

The final rule's text remains confidential until publication, so the percentile figures above are the proposed ones; the published rule could adopt them, modify them, and must respond to the public comments filed before the comment period closed on May 26, 2026. A near-identical wage rule issued at the end of the first Trump administration was challenged in court and never took effect — litigation is a realistic possibility again, though it cannot be assumed.

When — and what to do next

Three steps remain: OIRA review (no fixed length; the executive order framework allows up to 90 days), publication in the Federal Register, and — because this is a major rule under the Congressional Review Act — at least 60 days before it can take effect. Analysis of recent comparable reviews points to an effective date in spring 2027, though a fast clearance could bring it earlier; the binding date will be printed in the published rule. Under the proposal, labour condition applications filed before the effective date keep today's wages, while PERM prevailing-wage requests still pending on the effective date would get the new levels — which is why immigration counsel are advising employers to file wage requests and planned LCAs early rather than wait for the Federal Register.
